near_miss.lead: ON skóp himin ok jǫrð 'created heaven and earth' (merism)
near_miss.why_not: Christian creed rendering (creatorem caeli et terrae) in a conversion narrative; the Germanic heaven/earth merism (Vsp. upphiminn/jǫrð, Wessobrunn ero/ufhimil) is better witnessed elsewhere and the Greek history partners contain nothing comparable.

near_miss.lead: mice (mús ~ μῦς ~ mus) in a portent/destruction narrative
near_miss.why_not: Only the shared word for 'mouse'; the ON hagiographic miracle (vermin leaping out of a smashed idol) and Herodotus' field-mice gnawing bowstrings, or Cato's pest recipe, share no wording or construction.

near_miss.lead: ON prophecy: æigi man hann skorta vit ne ríki ... frægð ok mikla sœmd man hann vinna
near_miss.why_not: Prophecy of fame is thematically promising, but partners are a botanical description and a Lucretian simile; frægð/sœmd are not cognate with any κλέος/śrávas term, so no shared wording.

near_miss.lead: ON berjask við 'fight with' ~ ORu. бороти 'fight' (*bʰorH-); also ON hjarta ~ Gk καρδίη
near_miss.why_not: berjask ~ boroti(sę) is a lexical/semantic match (shared 'strike'>'fight') but not a collocation in congruent contexts (dissuasion from battle vs. Novgorodians offering to fight for the prince); heart words co-occur by chance (arrow in heart vs. ON idiom of lost courage). ON 'illu heilli heiman' has no partner.

near_miss.why_not: Contexts not congruent: ON mikit verk is a labour quota set for thralls (quantity of work), whereas Homeric/Herodotean μέγα ἔργον is a 'great (mis)deed'; big+work is generic in every branch.

near_miss.why_not: Sun + light/shine co-occurrence is universal; ON is a hagiographic miracle scene in prose with no figure shared with the Vedic dawn hymns. The AM-36-fol partner is the same ON episode in another redaction (same branch).
ON 'ill var hin fyrra fǫr ... sjá var hálfu verri' (narrative comparison) shares nothing with the Cato prayer or AV riddle hymn; frétta 'learn by asking' vs precor is root coincidence.

near_miss.lead: taking a child on one's knee(s): ON tekr sveininn í kné sér
near_miss.why_not: Slab partners use the knee word in other contexts (Hitt. sleep on the beloved's knees; Hom. knees = life), so no two slab anchors share the gesture; see search lead.

search_lead.cognate: ON kné ~ Gk γόνυ (γούνασι) ~ Hitt. genu- < *ǵónu; with a placing verb and a male child/kinsman
search_lead.argument: Setting a child on a man's knee(s) as an act of acknowledgement: in Od. 19.401 Eurykleia puts the newborn on Autolykos' knees and he names him; Il. 9.455 curses Phoenix never to have a son seated on his knees; ON knésetja/setja á kné is the fostering act (Hákon set on Æthelstan's knee, AM-35) and Óláfr sets his half-brothers on his knees to test them (pivot; AM-36). Cognate noun with the same act and kin context; but the gesture is near-universal, so the evidence lies in the legal-ritual function (naming, fosterage), which the pivot itself only hints at. Hittite (Ullikummi: Kumarbi sets the newborn on his knees, names him) is recalled, not found in the indexed corpus.

search_lead.cognate: no full cognate pair; ON hræ 'corpse' is perhaps cognate with Gk κρέας / Ved. kravíṣ- 'raw flesh' (*krewh₂-), not used in the Homeric lines
search_lead.argument: Same figure in the same speech act: a future-tense threat/prophecy to a man about to fall in battle that a carrion bird and a carrion canine (hrafnar ... ok vargar ~ κύνες ... οἰωνοί) will tear/divide his body. Lexically fully renewed, so only a thematic-formulaic parallel (the pairing is noted in the literature as inherited 'dogs and birds' theme).
